paper_title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations. We argue that anomalous steps can be identified by measuring the entropy deviation of each denoising step from its neighboring temporal window. We hypothesize that discrete token commitment discards the distributional information at masked positions, limiting the continued interaction between candidate semantics and the context during entropy spikes. With this goal, we present StepRefine, a plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages semantic context to achieve reliable denoising. The core of our method lies in a step-aware switch between discrete denoising and latent refinement. The model employs probability-weighted embeddings at entropy spike steps to preserve diverse reasoning hypotheses and performs multiple rounds of continuous refinement. Meanwhile, a refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary loops and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising. Through extensive experiments, StepRefine demonstrates significant hallucination mitigation across different MDLMs on multimodal benchmarks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion language models [40, 98, 19] replace autoregressive left-to-right generation with iterative denoising, forming an alternative paradigm for sequence generation. Current diffusion language models typically adopt discrete masked diffusion mechanism [54, 90, 105, 58], in which multiple masked positions are predicted in parallel and progressively committed to discrete tokens. This paradigm has recently been extended to multimodal settings. Multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) [92, 93, 39, 89, 65] leverage bidirectional attention over visual and textual inputs to model global context, demonstrating strong potential in perception and reasoning tasks. Despite these advantages, MDLMs remain susceptible to hallucination. Existing inference-time methods for diffusion language models primarily focus on efficiency, such as cache reuse [27, 79, 107] and denoising scheduling [46, 43, 29], but these methods typically do not improve sequence reliability. Other decoding strategies attempt to improve quality by modifying token commitment policies, for example, by re-masking unreliable tokens [22, 25] or introducing continuous token representations [103, 21, 10]. However, these methods typically treat uncertainty uniformly across denoising steps and do not explicitly account for temporal irregularities in the denoising trajectory. In this paper, we examine hallucination in MDLMs from the perspective of step-wise uncertainty dynamics across denoising steps. natural expectation is that predictive uncertainty should steadily decrease as the sequence becomes progressively less masked and the context becomes more complete. Our analysis shows that the average entropy of the masked sequence indeed decreases. However, this decrease is not monotonic. small number of steps show sharp entropy increases relative to their local temporal window. We refer to these steps as entropy spikes. Through statistical analysis, entropy spike steps are rare but highly correlated with hallucinated tokens in the final response. We observe that entropy spike steps exhibit non-uniform distribution along the denoising trajectory, mainly occurring in the early-to-middle stages. At these stages, large portion of the sequence remains masked, leaving the context information still limited. Moreover, we find that replacing standard confidence-based decoding with random decoding at entropy spike steps causes little performance change, whereas applying the same perturbation at ordinary steps results in clear degradation. At entropy spike steps, confidence signals may become less discriminative, making discrete decoding less reliably grounded in the current context. Therefore, our findings suggest that identifying entropy spike steps and applying contextual refinement before discrete commitment is crucial to mitigating hallucinations. In this work, we propose StepRefine, plug-and-play decoding strategy that leverages dense contextual cues to improve denoising reliability. StepRefine adaptively switches between standard discrete denoising and latent probabilistic refinement based on the entropy dynamics of each step from its local temporal window. Specifically, StepRefine computes the average mask entropy at each denoising step and detects entropy spikes by comparing the current entropy change against trends within local window. When such spikes are detected, the model switches to probabilistic refinement mode, constructs probability-weighted token embeddings that implicitly preserve diverse hypotheses, and promotes sufficient interaction between candidate semantics and the context through iterative refinement. In addition, refinement controller monitors distributional stability to reduce unnecessary iterations and switch the model back to standard discrete denoising when appropriate. Extensive experiments show that StepRefine significantly reduces hallucinations across multiple MDLM models on diverse reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our main contributions are as follows: We analyze the relationship between entropy spike steps and hallucinations in multimodal diffusion models from the perspective of uncertainty dynamics across denoising steps. We propose StepRefine, plug-and-play decoding approach that mitigates hallucinations through entropy spike detection and step-aware mode switching. Extensive evaluations across four MDLM backbones and diverse multimodal benchmarks show the superior performance of StepRefine, offering an effective solution for multimodal diffusion hallucinations.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Settings Baselines and Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate StepRefine on four representative MDLMs (LLaDA-V-8B [92], LLaDA-O-8B [93], Dream-VL-7B [89], and LaViDa-L-8B [39]). We evaluate on diverse suite of multimodal benchmarks covering four general and domain-specific reasoning categories: (i) General reasoning & understanding on VStar [77], MMVP [66], MMEval-Pro [24], VMCBench [100], RealWorldQA [80]; (ii) General hallucination assessment on MMHalu [62], Bingo [14], POPE [42], (iii) Mathematical reasoning on MathVision [69], MathVista [47]; and (iv) Scientific reasoning on the MMK12 [52] Physics and Chemistry subsets. Implementation Details. Across all backbones and benchmarks, we decode with generation length = 256, total denoising steps = 256, and low-confidence remasking. The stability threshold ϵ is set to 0.01. Details of the compared methods are provided in Appendix B.1. 4.2 Main Results Benchmark Evaluation. We compare StepRefine against three training-free decoding strategies for MDLMs, including CoTA [101], ReMix [91], and WINO [22], as shown in Table 1. On LLaDAV-8B, StepRefine improves average accuracy on general reasoning by +2.8% over the baseline and matches or outperforms competing decoding strategies on every general reasoning benchmark. It also improves on the hallucination benchmarks, yielding gains of +2.5% on MMHalu and +4.4% on Bingo. These improvements generalize across all backbones and benchmark categories. Additional results are reported in Appendix B.3. Compatibility with Acceleration Methods. We further evaluate StepRefine in combination with three acceleration methods, including Fast-dLLM [75], dLLM-Cache [44], dKV-Cache [51]. StepRefine is orthogonal to these methods by design. Each refinement round, StepRefine operates on the embedding at masked positions through standard forward passes, leaving the cache and feature-reuse schedules used by each accelerator unchanged during ordinary steps. Table 2 shows that, plugged into each method, StepRefine largely maintains the speedups of these acceleration methods while improving performance by +2.9% on VStar and +1.6% on MMHalu. Throughput is also preserved or slightly increased after adding StepRefine, confirming that refinement does not introduce hidden latency. The additional speedup over each accelerators baseline is due to the budget compensation mechanism. The refinement rounds at an entropy spike step are charged against the remaining step budget, replacing later steps rather than extending the total compute. Qualitative Analysis. Figure 3 illustrates representative StepRefine decoding trajectory, which alternates between standard denoising steps and entropy spike steps. Within each spike step, we plot the predicted distributions at masked positions across the refinement rounds. As refinement proceeds, these distributions sharpen as the entropy of the predicted distribution decreases, and the prediction converges on the candidate that is finally committed. Each refinement round feeds the soft embeddings derived from the previous distributions back into the model, letting competing candidates interact with the surrounding context. 4.3 Ablation Study Effect of Calibration Window Size. We study the effect of the calibration window size used for entropy spike detection. As shown in Fig. 4, accuracy improves as the window increases up to moderate size (w = 16 in our experiments), and then oscillates. When the window is small, the entropy-deviation estimate is dominated by step-to-step noise and produces unstable triggers. When the window is large, entropy deviations are averaged across denoising stages with different uncertainty profiles, blurring the distinction between stable steps and steps with entropy spike. Taken together, these suggest that moderate window provides reasonable trade-off in our setting. Adaptive versus Fixed Refinement Scheduling. We compare StepRefines adaptive trigger against three fixed schedules that insert latent refinement at uniformly spaced denoising steps. Fig. 5(a) reveals that the adaptive trigger outperforms all three fixed schedules. Entropy spike steps neither follow uniform spacing nor occur at the same positions across samples, so periodic schedule may fail to capture spikes in some inputs while spending refinement on already-stable steps in others. In contrast, our adaptive trigger conditions both the position and frequency of refinement on local entropy deviation, applying refinement only at steps with anomalous uncertainty. sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Multimodal diffusion LLM. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) [54, 90, 105, 28, 1] leverage their inherent bidirectional attention and iterative denoising process to exhibit strong global context modeling capability and flexible reasoning potential. In recent years, this paradigm has been further extended to multimodal settings. Multimodal diffusion models [20, 38, 65, 6, 26, 74, 89, 34, 12] are typically built upon pretrained dLLMs and incorporate visual representations to handle visionlanguage tasks. For example, methods such as LLaDA-V [92], LaViDa [39], and Dimple [94] align image features into the same embedding space as text tokens through visual instruction tuning, enabling joint modeling of visual and linguistic information. Another line of methods [88, 63, 59], such as LLaDA-O [93], Lumina-dimoo [84], and LaViDa-O [37], further combines fine-tuning and reinforcement learning to jointly model discretized visual and textual representations for unified multimodal generation and understanding. In addition, methods such as DiffusionVL [95] and Fudoki [67] transform autoregressive models into the discrete diffusion paradigm through diffusion fine-tuning, providing another path for multimodal diffusion modeling. Decoding strategy in dLLM. Despite the advantages of parallel generation and global modeling offered by discrete masked diffusion, the inference efficiency [55, 53, 23, 18, 78, 75, 9, 3] and generation quality of diffusion large language models largely depend on the decoding strategy. One line of work leverages cache reuse [32, 27, 71, 61, 51, 44] and token pruning [45, 82, 41, 8, 4] to alleviate the computational bottlenecks introduced by global attention. Another line of research focuses on optimizing sampling [16, 81, 5, 35, 15, 31, 68, 56, 70, 30], early stopping [36, 33, 7], and step scheduling [49, 99, 17, 73, 17, 99, 2, 50] to reduce redundant denoising iterations. Existing approaches for mitigating hallucinations in diffusion models include self-corrective decoding [22, 25, 64, 11, 60, 83, 104] and prior constraints [108, 13, 76, 57, 85, 96, 87], which improve model reliability by reducing error accumulation. Prior work replaces the binary mask-to-token transition with continuous token representations at each decoding step [91, 106, 103, 10, 21, 102]. We examine hallucination in MDLMs from the perspective of step-wise uncertainty dynamics during denoising. Based on this observation, we propose StepRefine, plug-and-play decoding method that mitigates hallucinations by detecting entropy spike steps and selectively applying latent refinement.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we extensively study hallucination in multimodal diffusion language models by looking at how predictive uncertainty evolves across denoising steps. We observe that during iterative denoising, MDLMs show sharp local increases in mean mask entropy at small number of steps, which we call entropy spikes. These steps correlate with hallucinated tokens and mainly arise in the early-to-middle stages of denoising, where confidence-based decoding becomes less reliably 9 grounded in the current context. Building on this observation, we introduce StepRefine, training-free decoding strategy that detects entropy spikes via local trend deviation, switches to iterative latent refinement at those steps, and adaptively terminates once the predictive distribution stabilizes. Across four MDLM backbones and multiple benchmarks comprehensively covering general reasoning, hallucination, mathematical, and scientific reasoning, StepRefine obtains improved accuracy and can be combined with existing acceleration methods. In summary, our findings suggest that focusing refinement on small number of high-uncertainty steps yields measurable improvements in MDLM decoding without additional training.

sections.title: A Use of LLMs
sections.content: LLMs were used solely as writing and editing assistants in this study, with their role limited to improving grammar, spelling, clarity, and stylistic consistency. They did not contribute to the scientific content of the work, including research ideation, experimental design, data analysis, result interpretation, or any core intellectual contributions. All substantive content and scientific contributions are entirely attributable to the authors.

sections.title: B Additional Experiments
sections.content: B.1 Baseline All experiments are conducted on single server with 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80GB). To benchmark our method against recent training-free decoding strategies for diffusion-based models, we reproduce three representative baselines. All baselines are implemented under the same backbone and evaluation pipeline. We follow the original method designs and reported hyper-parameter settings whenever available to ensure fair comparison. Wide-In, Narrow-Out (WINO) [22]: WINO enables revokable decoding for DLLMs through parallel draft-and-verify mechanism. At each decoding step, it first drafts multiple tokens using lenient confidence threshold, then verifies previously decoded tokens with an auxiliary shadow block and re-masks low-confidence tokens for refinement. We follow the original semi-autoregressive decoding setting and use the reported drafting and verification thresholds. Context Tokens are Anchors (CoTA) [101]: CoTA mitigates cache-induced repetition in dMLLMs by preserving the information flow of context tokens. It enhances attention to nearby context tokens through distance-aware intervention and adjusts decoding scores using deep-layer context-token entropy to suppress uncertain candidates. We integrate CoTA with the corresponding cache setting and follow the original hyper-parameter configuration. Rejection Mixing (ReMix) [91]: ReMix accelerates DLLM decoding by introducing continuous mixing state between masked and finalized token states. Undecoded positions are updated with probability-weighted embeddings to propagate semantic information, while unstable positions are rejected back to the masked state based on distributional divergence. We follow the original confidence threshold, mixing ratio, and rejection threshold settings. We also examine the compatibility of our method with recent training-free inference acceleration methods for diffusion language models. These methods target different computational bottlenecks during diffusion decoding, such as feature reuse, KV-cache approximation, sparse attention, and delayed cache updates. Since our method only introduces an intra-step soft refinement before discrete token commitment, these acceleration methods can be applied during regular denoising steps and resumed after refinement. dLLM-Cache [44]: dLLM-Cache accelerates diffusion language model inference by reusing intermediate features across adjacent denoising steps. It applies long-interval caching to static prompt tokens and adaptive short-interval updates to response tokens, where dynamically changing positions are selected according to value-vector similarity. When combined with our method, dLLM-Cache can be used during regular decoding steps, while soft-refinement steps are handled with an isolated temporary cache before refreshing the main cache after token commitment. Fast-dLLM [75]: Fast-dLLM improves diffusion LLM inference through block-wise approximate KV caching and confidence-aware parallel decoding. Its cache mechanism reuses prefix, or prefix-and-suffix, KV states within decoding block, while its parallel decoding strategy commits only high-confidence tokens to reduce dependency errors. In our setting, Fast-dLLM can operate during normal decoding, whereas soft refinement temporarily disables cache reuse and then returns the refined logits to the standard confidence-aware commitment rule. SparseD [72]: SparseD reduces the quadratic attention cost in diffusion language models by using head-specific sparse attention patterns. It first applies full attention in early denoising 18 steps, then pre-computes sparse query-key patterns and reuses them in later steps. Since SparseD modifies the attention computation rather than the discrete decoding trajectory, it is naturally compatible with our method; during soft refinement, one may either retain the sparse attention pattern or conservatively fall back to full attention. dKV-Cache [51]: dKV-Cache introduces delayed KV-cache mechanism for diffusion language models by caching only decoded tokens whose representations have become relatively stable. To avoid instability immediately after token commitment, it delays cache insertion by one denoising step and periodically refreshes cached states. When integrated with our method, dKV-Cache remains active in regular denoising steps, while refinement uses temporary soft-state cache; newly committed tokens after refinement follow the original one-step delayed caching rule. B.2 Benchmarks In this section, we briefly describe each benchmark used in our evaluation, grouped into four categories: general reasoning, hallucination, mathematical reasoning, and scientific reasoning. B.2.1 General Reasoning & Understanding V*Bench (vstar_bench) [77]: multimodal benchmark built on diverse real-world images that probes visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and fine-grained attribute recognition in VLMs. RealWorldQA [80]: collection of real-world photographs (many taken from vehicle viewpoints) paired with short-answer questions, targeting basic spatial understanding and everyday scene reasoning. MMVP (MultiModal Visual Patterns) [66]: 300 carefully crafted questions over CLIPblind image pairs, testing whether models can tell apart subtle visual-pattern differences that standard visual encoders typically miss. MMEval-Pro [24]: calibrated multimodal benchmark that augments existing multiplechoice datasets (e.g., MMMU, ScienceQA, MathVista) with perception and knowledgeanchor questions, forming question triplets that suppress text-only shortcuts. VMCBench [100]: unified multiple-choice benchmark (9k questions) that consolidates 20 VQA datasets via AutoConverter, enabling consistent and scalable evaluation of VLMs across diverse visual-linguistic scenarios. B.2.2 Hallucination Benchmark MMHalu (MMHal-Bench) [62]: general-purpose hallucination benchmark built on diverse image-question pairs, measuring how often models generate visually inconsistent or fabricated content in realistic settings. Bingo (Bias and Interference Challenges) [14]: diagnostic benchmark with image-text challenge sets that target bias-driven errors (region, OCR, factual) together with interferenceinduced hallucinations. POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) [42]: an object-hallucination probe built from balanced yes/no questions about object existence, providing stable, instructionagnostic measure of image-faithful generation. B.2.3 Mathematical Reasoning MathVision (MATH-Vision) [69]: 3,040 visual math problems drawn from real competitions, spanning 16 disciplines and 5 difficulty levels, to assess multimodal mathematical reasoning in exam-style settings. MathVista [47]: unified benchmark of 6,141 examples from 28 existing datasets together with three new subsets (IQTest, FunctionQA, PaperQA), evaluating mathematical reasoning over diagrams, plots, and scientific figures. MathVerse [97]: 2,612 diagram-based math problems expanded into 15k multimodal variants, enabling fine-grained evaluation of whether MLLMs actually reason over diagrams rather than rely on text alone. 19 VisuLogic [86]: 1,000 single-choice visual reasoning problems across six categories (quantitative shifts, spatial relations, attribute comparisons, etc.), explicitly designed to rule out language-only shortcuts. Geometry3K [48]: 3,002 multiple-choice Euclidean geometry problems paired with diagrams and formalized structural annotations, covering high-school to competition-level difficulty. B.2.4 Scientific Reasoning MMK12 [52]: K-12 multimodal reasoning dataset from the MM-Eureka framework; its evaluation split contains 500 multiple-choice questions per discipline (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology), covering foundational scientific reasoning. sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Our contributions are summarized in the Abstract and Introduction sections. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We discuss failure cases in Appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] 26 Justification: This paper does not include theoretical results. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Please see the setup in Sec.4.1 and detailed experimental settings in appendix B. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? 27 Answer: [Yes] Justification: The code will be released upon acceptance. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The detailed results can be found in Appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The detailed results can be found in Appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. 28 It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The detailed results can be found in Appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have read the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and confirm that our research complies with these ethical standards. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Please see the Appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. 29 The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper poses no such risks. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All the thing in this paper credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper does not release new assets. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage 31 Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [N/A] Justification: The method development in this paper does not involve LLMs as any components. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
